content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published updated treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) in 2016. These guidelines focus on the management of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), providing evidence-based recommendations for healthcare professionals worldwide. The document includes updates on the optimal combination of medications, the use of shorter treatment regimens, the role of surgical interventions, and the impact of treatment delays on outcomes. The guidelines were developed by a multidisciplinary Guideline Development Group (GDG) composed of TB and drug-resistant TB experts external to WHO. The GDG met in November 2015 to review the latest evidence and formulate recommendations. The scope of the 2016 update included the following key areas: 1. Optimal Treatment Regimens: Recommendations were made for the design of treatment regimens for patients with isoniazid-resistant TB, rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), MDR-TB, and XDR-TB. This included both adults and children, as well as patients with Mycobacterium bovis disease. 2. Shorter MDR-TB Regimens: A shorter treatment regimen lasting 9–12 months was conditionally recommended for patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB who had not been previously treated with second-line drugs and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents was excluded or considered highly unlikely. 3. Longer MDR-TB Regimens: For patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB, a longer regimen with at least five effective TB medications during the intensive phase was recommended. This included pyrazinamide and four core second-line TB drugs, with specific guidance on the selection of medications based on updated evidence. 4. Surgical Interventions: Elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) was conditionally recommended as an adjunct to medical treatment for patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB. 5. Treatment Delays: The guidelines addressed the impact of delays in initiating treatment for drug-resistant TB, emphasizing the importance of timely intervention to improve outcomes. The 2016 update also introduced changes to the classification of medications used in MDR-TB treatment regimens. Clofazimine and linezolid were reclassified as core second-line medications, while p-aminosalicylic acid was designated as an add-on agent. Additionally, bedaquiline and delamanid were assigned to a specific subgroup of add-on agents, with bedaquiline recommended only for adults and delamanid approved for use in patients aged 6–17 years. The recommendations were informed by systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and individual patient data analyses. For adults, the treatment regimen recommendations were based on data from over 9,000 patients, while recommendations for children were supported by data from 974 pediatric patients. Evidence on shorter MDR-TB regimens was derived from studies conducted in Asia and Africa, and surgical recommendations were based on individual patient data and study-level meta-analyses. The guidelines also highlighted areas where evidence was insufficient to make specific recommendations, such as the treatment of isoniazid-resistant TB, the management of M. bovis disease, and the impact of treatment delays. The 2011 recommendations for these areas remain applicable until further evidence becomes available. The development of the guidelines involved extensive collaboration and input from experts, external reviewers, and WHO staff. Funding for the update was provided by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). In summary, the 2016 WHO guidelines for drug-resistant TB provide updated, evidence-based recommendations to optimize the treatment and care of patients with MDR-TB and XDR-TB. These updates reflect the latest scientific evidence and aim to support healthcare professionals in addressing the ongoing challenges posed by drug-resistant TB.
